title: Weather at Gettysburg, June 25 to July 8, 1863, from Michael Jacobs's record and his own narrative
status: Verified as far as the sources allow; see verification_summary and warnings. The numbers are second-hand: the original observation forms were not seen.

badge_legend.Measured: an instrument reading (thermometer, rain gauge) by the observer; here relayed second-hand
badge_legend.Observed: a trained observer's eye estimate recorded in his log (cloud cover and type, wind direction and force, thunder)
badge_legend.Reported: a narrative statement by a witness, not a log entry
badge_legend.Computed: derived from an ephemeris (none in this file; see astro_by_day.json)
badge_legend.Modelled: an estimate from a model (none in this file; a heat index would be Modelled and is not included)
badge_legend.Contested: two or more sources disagree and none is chosen

site.name: Gettysburg, Pennsylvania (Pennsylvania College, the observer's station)
site.note: The readings were taken in the town by Michael Jacobs; the thermometer exposure is not recorded in these sources (the pitch's remark that it was in shade is an inference).

holdings.what: Mss 551.5.j12, "Meteorological Observations Made for the Franklin Institute 1839-1865": an original set of Jacobs’s daily forms (his retained copy), per Harding
RG 27, Microfilm Publication T907, Reel 445: microfilm of the forms Jacobs submitted to the Smithsonian (almost all of them); no monthly reports for August 1863 to June 1864
microfilm copies of the same forms, per Harding; the NCEI catalogue record says its images are under "Controlled user access to the NERMS system"
Michael Jacobs Collection, MS-107, and VFM 386: named in Harding’s list of archives; what it holds of the weather record is not stated in the cached page

where_the_readings_are.july_1863_form: Harding says he compared the July 1863 forms at NCEI/NARA and at the APS and that they carry the same information (X-tge-july). So the form that would settle the wind speed (2 against 12 miles per hour, C-wind-jul1) and the first rain figure exists in at least two places. [OWNER TO PROVIDE: a read of the July 1 to July 4 1863 form from the APS or from NARA microfilm T907 reel 445; no NCEI image may be displayed without written permission.]
where_the_readings_are.statement: Michael Jacobs observed three times a day for the Smithsonian Institution. Copies of his forms are said to be at the American Philosophical Society (Franklin Institute series, per the Gettysburg Experience article), and as microfilm at NARA and NCEI. This project saw none of them. What it holds is the 1885 article by his son.
evidence: Gettysburg Experience, "Dr. Michael Jacobs: Gettysburg's Weatherman" (https://www.thegettysburgexperience.com/dr-michael-jacobs-gettysburgs-weatherman), read 2026-10-04: the oft-quoted source is the article "Meteorology of the Battle" that comes through the professor's son 22 years after the battle.
HistoryNet interview with Jeffrey J. Harding (https://historynet.com/gettysburg-heat/), read 2026-10-04: his original records were more detailed than the version published by his son in 1885.

external_statements.text: Controlled user access to the NERMS system
Observations were generally conducted three times daily, around 7am, 2pm and 9pm.
The original forms were deteriorating in the National Archives and were converted to microfilm in the late 1930s as part of a Works Projects Administration program.
the oft quoted primary source of weather conditions during the battle is an article entitled Meteorology of the Battle, that comes to us through the professor’s son 22 years after the battle
external_statements.note: Jeffrey J. Harding, Gettysburg Experience Magazine (second-hand: a magazine article, not a record). Supports the finding that the numbers in circulation come from H. E. Jacobs’s 1885 article, not from the 1864 Notes.

external_statements.text: included an original set of Professor Jacobs’s original daily weather observation records, both those made for the Franklin Institute and those made on behalf of the Smithsonian Institution
external_statements.note: Harding on the American Philosophical Society collection "Meteorological Observations Made for the Franklin Institute 1839-1865". Not seen by this project.

external_statements.text: both the NCEI and the National Archives held microfilm copies of almost all of Professor Jacobs’s daily observation records obtained on behalf of the Smithsonian Institution
external_statements.note: Not seen by this project; the NCEI images are controlled-access.

external_statements.text: When comparing the daily weather observation forms for July of 1863 (NCEI/NA copies vs. APS originals), one can readily see that the same information is presented save for certain highlighted items.
external_statements.note: Harding says he compared the July 1863 forms at both places: the form for the battle month exists in both. He prints no readings from it in the page that was cached.

external_statements.text: All of the records for these months, save for August 1863, can be found in the APS collection.
external_statements.note: The months meant, from the sentence before: NCEI and the National Archives lack the monthly reports for August to December 1863 and January to June 1864 (so August 1863 is held by neither). July 1863, the battle month, is not among the missing months.

external_statements.text: Meteorological observations made for the Franklin Institute 1839-1865, Mss 551.5.j12. Gettysburg College, Musselman Library Archives. Michael Jacobs Collection, MS-107, and VFM 386. National Archives. RG 27, Microfilm Publication T907, Reel 445.
external_statements.note: The call numbers in Harding’s list of archives. Which of these holds which month is stated only in the sentences above.
Harding reports that Jacobs wrote these words on his July 1863 report; a second-hand report of a form note, not a reading of the form.

external_statements.text: Jacobs’ original records were more detailed than the secondary source version of his records that was published by his son (Henry Eyster Jacobs) in 1885
external_statements.note: Harding in a HistoryNet interview: the original forms (in the NCEI FORTS database) hold more than the 1885 article.

The MRCC list of keyed (digitised) FORTS stations names these Pennsylvania stations: Blooming Grove, Canonsburg, Carlisle, Erie, Franklin, Germantown, Harrisburg, Morrisville, Philadelphia, Pittsburgh. Gettysburg is not among them, so there is no keyed copy of Jacobs's readings to cross-check against; the NCEI images are controlled-access and were never fetched.

quotes.text: Friday, June 26.
quotes.note: The paragraph about the heavy rain of the night (Q-N-rain-jun25) is the last before this heading, so it is Thursday June 25.
ocr_misses: copy C: the OCR text of that page does not match the quote exactly (a character-recognition slip)

quotes.text: But the heavy rain of that night caused them to be detained until the balance of the regiment arrived

Being wet from the rain which had fallen during the most of the day, and considerably heated by a long march, there was found, by a person near them as they passed, to have been more truth than fiction in the remark of a friend, that "the air was filled with the filthy exhalations from their bodies."
quotes.role: weather and smell remark about a marching Confederate brigade, NOT about the battlefield

quotes.text: General Early, who accompanied this brigade, and remained in town over Friday night
quotes.note: Friday night is the night of June 26; the "wet from the rain" passage is on the page before it and describes the same brigade.

quotes.text: Thursday, July 2.
at about sunset came the Sixth corps
The morning was pleasant, the air was calm, the sun shone mildly through a smoky atmosphere, and the whole outer world was quiet and peaceful
The enemy came up under cover of the forest and approaching darkness
At the dawn of day our artillery opened upon the Rebels
At sunrise this was followed by a general infantry attack
At seven minutes past 1 p. m., the awful and portentous silence was broken.
quotes.role: clock time of the opening of the cannonade (not weather)

quotes.text: such as were never equalled by the most terrific thunder-storm ever witnessed by mortal man
quotes.role: SIMILE for the noise of the guns, not a weather observation

quotes.text: From June 15th until July 22nd, 1863, there was not an entirely clear day.
June 25th, at 8 p. m., a rain began
This rain continued at intervals until Saturday, June 27th, at 7 a. m., the precipitation being in inches 1, - 280.
quotes.note: The figure is garbled in the transcription ("1, - 280"); read as 1.280 inches by analogy with the later figures "1.390" and "1.300"; the clipping image does not cover this paragraph.

quotes.text: At all the observations made on Saturday and Sunday, and until the nine o'clock observation of Monday night, the entire sky was covered with clouds.
On the day before the battle, both at 7 a. m., and 2 p. m., the obscuration was again complete, with cumulo-stratus clouds moving from S.S.E. At 9 p. m., only four-tenths of the heavens were covered.
During these days of sombre suspense, the records of the wind are those of almost an entire calm.
June 25th, 59 51 63

FIRST DAY.-All through the first day, the entire sky was covered with clouds, viz: cumulo-stratus at 7 a. m. and 2 p. m.; and cirro-stratus at 9 p. m. A very gentle southern breeze, (2 miles per hour).
Thermometer: 7 A.M. 2 P.M. 9 P.M. 72 76 74
SECOND DAY.-At 8 a. m., sky still covered, (cumulo-stratus). At 2 p. m., three-tenths are clear. At 9 p. m., there are cirrus clouds; wind as on preceding day.
Thermometer: 7 A.M. 2 P.M. 9 P.M. 74 81 76

THIRD DAY.-At 8 a. m., sky again completely covered with cumulo-stratus clouds; at 2 p. m., only four-tenths of the heavens are covered, but with cumulus or the massive thunder-cloud of summer; at 9 p. m., seven-tenths cumulus. Wind S. S. W., very gentle.
Thunder storm in neighborhood at 6 p. m. The thunder seemed tame, after the artillery firing of the afternoon.
Thermometer: 7 A.M. 2 P.M. 9 P.M. 73 87 76
SATURDAY, THE FOURTH.-Rain in showers at 6 a. m., from 2:15 to 4 p. m., and at 4 a. m. of the 5th, aggregating 1.390.
Thermometer: 7 A.M. 2 P.M. 9 P.M. 69 72 70
There were slight showers on the 5th and 7th; and on the 8th, a rain from 3 a. m. to 11:30 a. m., which measured 1.300.
The maximum temperature for the month of July 1863, was 87(, at the time of Pickett's charge. Eleven days of the month, the maximum was in the seventies, and on one day (17th) it was but sixty-two.
quotes.note: The degree sign is printed as a small raised circle (the transcription renders it "(").

quotes.text: The morning was thick and sultry, the sky overcast with low, vapory clouds
quotes.role: weather remark (morning of July 2, before six)
